quest_006_00.story:
At the edge of meteor stairways, Lin Lan waits until the last lantern is lit before speaking. Lin Lan is known as a winter scout, but that title has become a shelter for a different kind of work. Tonight Lin Lan has brought the silver star compass, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect a sister erased from the academy rolls to the curse spreading through Starfall Steps. Lin Lan asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Lin Lan explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Starfall Steps, where a pilgrimage built from fallen stars. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Qiao Wei remembers the night differently. Qiao Wei heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The star pilgrims later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Lin Lan wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called A Name in Water. Its immediate task is speak with Lin Lan. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Lin Lan insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Moonwell follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Lin Lan gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Qiao Wei explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Starfall Steps in the first place.

The creature called Silver Stag appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of charge. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Lin Lan once trusted the star pilgrims because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Qiao Wei asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns a sister erased from the academy rolls. Lin Lan has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Lin Lan chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near meteor stairways. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Lin Lan recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Silver Stag, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Qiao Wei proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Lin Lan refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Lin Lan teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Moonwell arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises belonging without possession while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Qiao Wei has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Lin Lan speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Silver Stag senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of speak with Lin Lan cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

After the immediate work, Qiao Wei asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Lin Lan gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The silver star compass now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Lin Lan wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through meteor stairways with the result of speak with Lin Lan. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Lin Lan records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Lin Lan offers a conversation rather than another command. Lin Lan asks Lin Yue whether belonging without possession can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Starfall Steps, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Qiao Wei receives a copy, Lin Lan retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.

The creature has a particular history: Each silver antler branch marks a winter in which the grain court denied that anyone had starved.
quest_006_00.mercy: Lin Lan records the result of the task to speak with Lin Lan. The account is witnessed rather than final: Qiao Wei receives a copy, and the next chapter follows the evidence carried by the silver star compass. The binding's final fate remains undecided.

Tonight Su Lian has brought the folded river map, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect a mother whose name was traded for medicine to the curse spreading through Starfall Steps. Su Lian asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Su Lian explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Starfall Steps, where a pilgrimage built from fallen stars. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Han Rui remembers the night differently. Han Rui heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The star pilgrims later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Su Lian wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called The Second Binding. Its immediate task is defeat 2 manifestations of Paper Crane Swarm. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Su Lian insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Lantern Harbor follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Su Lian gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Han Rui explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Starfall Steps in the first place.

The creature called Paper Crane Swarm appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of charge. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Su Lian once trusted the star pilgrims because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Han Rui asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns a mother whose name was traded for medicine. Su Lian has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Su Lian chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near meteor stairways. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Su Lian recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Paper Crane Swarm, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Han Rui proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Su Lian refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Su Lian teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Lantern Harbor arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises belonging without possession while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Han Rui has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Su Lian speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Paper Crane Swarm senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of defeat 2 manifestations of Paper Crane Swarm cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

After the immediate work, Han Rui asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Su Lian gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The folded river map now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Su Lian wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through meteor stairways with the result of defeat 2 manifestations of Paper Crane Swarm. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Su Lian records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Su Lian offers a conversation rather than another command. Su Lian asks Lin Yue whether belonging without possession can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Starfall Steps, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Han Rui receives a copy, Su Lian retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.

The creature has a particular history: Each crane carries one line of an apology that the emperor ordered folded away before it could be delivered.
quest_042_07.mercy: Su Lian records the result of the task to defeat 2 manifestations of Paper Crane Swarm. The account is witnessed rather than final: Han Rui receives a copy, and the next chapter follows the evidence carried by the folded river map. The binding's final fate remains undecided.
